children: Jindal Steel highlights up to 90 per cent domestic sourcing for new gasification equipment, while industry experts flag high-ash Indian coal, project economics and carbon management as key considerations for commercial deployment

India’s coal gasification ambitions will depend on lowering capital costs, strengthening domestic equipment manufacturing and integrating carbon management solutions, industry executives said at Gasification India 2026 in New Delhi, as the country seeks to reduce dependence on imported industrial inputs and make greater use of domestic coal resources.

Speaking at the 17th edition of the conference, held on 22-23 October, Naveen Ahlawat, Head – Green Hydrogen, Green Steel, Gasification Projects and CCSU at Jindal Steel Limited, said the company’s experience with coal gasification highlighted the importance of supply-chain localisation and technology optimisation in making projects commercially viable.

Ahlawat said Jindal Steel had reduced its dependence on imported equipment and components for its ongoing gasification expansion, with domestic sourcing now accounting for around 90 per cent  of requirements, compared with approximately 55 per cent when the earlier plant was developed. “Cost is super important. The project cost, and everybody is aware that the growth of this project is capital expenditure-heavy. Optimisation, localisation of the supply chain, and reducing the cost are super important,” he said.

Ahlawat said the company was applying lessons from its existing coal gasification operations to a new phase of development, including manufacturing gasifiers and associated equipment within India. The initiative also involves using steel plates produced at its own steel plant and working with domestic suppliers to reduce dependence on imported components. He said the company was also evaluating changes to gas purification technology to bring down investment requirements.

According to Ahlawat, replacing the Rectisol process with pressure swing adsorption (PSA) for syngas-based direct reduced iron production could substantially reduce costs where the more complex purification process is unnecessary. The localisation push comes as India explores coal gasification for producing synthesis gas, or syngas, a mixture primarily comprising hydrogen and carbon monoxide. Syngas can serve as an industrial feedstock and reducing agent in steelmaking, while also supporting the production of chemicals and other industrial products.

Ahlawat said coal gasification could help reduce exposure to imported industrial inputs, but stressed that project developers must assess coal characteristics, technology maturity, conversion efficiency and the value of by-products before committing capital. He also pointed to opportunities to use syngas in existing industrial processes, including blast furnaces and galvanising and colour-coating lines, potentially reducing the consumption of other fuels.

However, the commercial case for coal gasification cannot be separated from its emissions profile, particularly as steelmakers face increasing pressure to decarbonise production. Ahlawat said gasification should be viewed as a transitional step rather than a substitute for the eventual shift towards green hydrogen and lower-carbon industrial processes. He cautioned that without integration with renewable energy and carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), coal gasification’s carbon intensity could remain comparable to conventional coal-based processes.
“Gasification has to be looked at as a bridge fuel or as a bridge step,” he said, adding that the longer-term direction for the steel sector remained lower-carbon production.

Hidayatullah Mohammad, Senior Engineer – Gasification Technology at Air Products, said the quality of Indian coal presented a significant technical and economic challenge because of its high ash content and the resulting demands on gasification systems. An internal assessment by Air Products, cited by Mohammad, found that increasing coal ash content from 16 per cent to 32 per cent raised coal consumption by around 34-35 per cent and oxygen consumption by approximately 20 per cent to produce the same quantity of syngas. Mohammad said technology selection and reactor design therefore needed to account for local coal characteristics, ash behaviour and the economics of operating the plant.

“It will never be a technology limitation to handle any challenging coal. We just have to see what is the right economic model that can fit in, and we have to choose the right design basis for that,” he said. Vartika Shukla, former Chairman and Managing Director of Engineers India Limited, chaired the session on advancing coal gasification technologies for commercial deployment. The discussions highlighted the central challenge facing India’s gasification strategy: translating domestic resource availability into commercially competitive industrial production while limiting emissions and reducing dependence on imported technology and equipment.
